h: Witches, a horse's tail and a song the whole world sings
p: Burns was born on 25 January 1759, and that date is celebrated every year with Burns Night suppers around the globe, complete with haggis, neeps and tatties and plenty of poetry. He also wrote the words to Auld Lang Syne, so if you have ever linked arms at New Year, you have already joined in with his work.

Before you visit, it is worth knowing the tale of Tam o' Shanter. Tam, riding home late after a night in the pub, stumbles across witches dancing in Alloway Kirk. He is chased by them to the Brig o' Doon, and only escapes because witches cannot cross running water, though his poor mare, Meg, loses her tail in the process. Walking from the kirk to the old bridge with that story in mind brings the whole village to life.
Burns's father, William, is buried in the Alloway kirkyard, so look out for his gravestone too.

The Poet's Path links the museum to the cottage, with quirky sculptures along the way, and it is a nice, easy walk for families. Allow two to three hours to enjoy the museum, cottage, monument and bridge without rushing.
Ayr itself has a long sandy beach and a lively town centre. Further down the coast, Culzean Castle, perched on clifftops above the sea, is a cracking addition to a South Ayrshire trip.
